meaning: The Exalted One (from Old Irish Brigit)

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b] and slender (palatalized) trill [rʲ]; Old Irish r was always palatalized after an initial b in this name, as in modern Irish.
Short front [i], held brief; in the later language the vowel lengthened, giving modern Irish Bríd.
Voiced velar fricative [ɣ] between vowels — not a hard stop but a soft continuant, the sound Old Irish wrote g in medial position.
Short front [i] and slender dental [dʲ]; the final d was devoiced and palatalized, surviving as the -d of modern Bríd /bʲrʲiːdʲ/.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BRIJ-id' — like 'bridge' split in two, the g softened to a voiced fricative (a gargled g), both r and d slender; the modern Irish form Bríd is simply 'breed'.

kin.label: Old Irish
kin.form: Brigit (genitive Brigte), daughter of the Dagda in the Mythological Cycle.

kin.label: Proto-Celtic
kin.form: *Brigantī, 'the Exalted One', source also of the tribal name Brigantes and the Romano-British goddess Brigantia.

kin.label: Scottish Gaelic and Manx

pronunciation.note: Brigid is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized form is already plain ASCII — the Old Irish spelling Brigit carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Only the capital distinguishes the temple's form from the input; the name's fame, like Baldr's, vastly outruns its orthography.

domains.title: The Exalted One
domains.subtitle: Poetry, Smithcraft, Healing — and the Undying Flame of Kildare
domains.lead: Brigit, daughter of the Dagda, is the triple hearth of the Irish gods: Cormac's Glossary gives her two sisters of the same name — Brigit the smith and Brigit the leech beside Brigit the poet — so that the one name covers the forge, the well, and the word. Her feast is Imbolc, the first of February, when the ewes come into milk; and at Kildare a fire burned for her, Giraldus says, that no man might approach and no night ever saw go out.

cards.name: The Sacred Flame
cards.desc: The perpetual fire of Kildare, tended by nineteen nuns in turn — on the twentieth night, Giraldus says, it was left to Brigid herself.

cards.name: The Anvil
cards.desc: Smithcraft, one of the three provinces Cormac assigns to the sisterhood of Brigits — the forge where Goibniu's art and mortal craft meet.

cards.name: The Poet's Harp
cards.desc: The first of her provinces in the Glossary — Brigit banfhiled, Brigit the woman-poet, patroness of the learned craft of filidecht.

cards.name: The Rush Cross
cards.desc: St Brigid's cross, woven of rushes on Imbolc eve — the small loom on which the goddess's feast was carried into the saint's day.

symbols.name: The flame of Kildare
symbols.meaning: The fire that neither dies nor accumulates ash — patronage that outlasts the night-watch of its keepers

symbols.name: The anvil and the forge
symbols.meaning: Smithcraft, the making province — skill that transforms raw metal the way poetry transforms raw speech

symbols.name: The holy well
symbols.meaning: Healing drawn from the ground — the countless wells of St Brigit where the leech-sister's province is still visited

symbols.name: Fea and Femen, the two oxen
symbols.meaning: The Dagda's daughter's beasts, who gave their names to plains of Ireland — wealth and the working land

symbols.name: Imbolc
symbols.meaning: The first of February, the milk returning to the ewes — the year's first hinge, kept as her day

mythology.lead: Irish tradition gives Brigit few long tales but a peculiar density of testimony: the great pseudohistory of the Lebor Gabála knows her genealogy, the battle-tale Cath Maige Tuired gives her the first keening heard in Ireland, and Cormac's Glossary preserves the triad that made her three goddesses in one name.

myths.title: The Dagda's Daughter
myths.text: The Book of Invasions places Brigit firmly in the family of the Túatha Dé Danann: Brigit the poetess, daughter of the Dagda, the good god who owns the cauldron and the club. The same tradition marries her to Bres, the half-Fomorian king whose beautiful face and niggardly rule nearly undid the Túatha Dé Danann, and gives her a son, Ruadán — so that the exalted one stands, by marriage and blood, on both sides of the great conflict of Irish myth. The Lebor Gabála is pseudohistory, written by Christian scholars ordering the gods into an ancestry, but its genealogies are the tradition's own filing system: Brigit belongs to the Dagda's house.

myths.title: Three Sisters, One Name
myths.text: Cormac mac Cuilennáin's glossary, compiled around 900, preserves the tradition's clearest statement of her triple nature. Brigit, it says, is the poetess, daughter of the Dagda — and she had two sisters, Brigits also: Brigit the woman of smithcraft and Brigit the female physician, from whose names all the Irish used to call a goddess Brigit. Three crafts, three sisters, one name: from this single entry comes the familiar picture of the triple goddess of poetry, smithcraft, and healing. Whether the triad records three genuinely distinct figures or one goddess's three provinces arranged in the Irish love of threes, the Glossary is the witness every later account follows.

myths.title: The First Keening in Ireland
myths.text: The Second Battle of Mag Tuired gives Brigit her one moment of action, and it is grief. Her son Ruadán, sent by his Fomorian kin to spy on the Túatha Dé Danann, hurls a spear at the smith Goibniu; the smith draws it from his own wound and casts it back, and Ruadán goes to his father to die. Brigit comes to the field and bewails her son — and the text says she wept and shrieked over him, the first keening and the first whistling for grief that was heard in Ireland. The inventor of lamentation is a terrible dignity: the goddess of the word is the one who first taught Ireland what a mother says at a grave.

myths.title: The Fire at Kildare
myths.text: Writing about 1188, Gerald of Wales describes the wonder of Kildare with a traveller's precision: a fire hedged round with a circular fence of brushwood, which no male may cross — any man who tries, he says, does not escape Brigid's vengeance. Nineteen nuns tend the flame, one each night, each adding fuel; on the twentieth night the last nun lays the wood and says, 'Brigid, guard your fire, it is yours.' In the morning the fire is found still burning, and its ashes, Gerald marvels, never increase though the wood is always consumed. He records it as a marvel of the saint's church; scholarship has never doubted that the hedge, the number nineteen, and the unashing flame belong to a far older hearth.

myths.title: Imbolc, the Ewe's Milk
myths.text: Her feast stands at Imbolc, the first of February, one of the four great hinges of the Irish year beside Beltaine, Lugnasad, and Samain. Cormac's Glossary explains the word itself as oimelc, 'ewe's milk' — the season when the sheep come into milk and the year's hunger begins to turn. The old texts keep the day as Brigit's own; the keening, the forge, and the word all gather at the one date, when the light is just beginning to return and the flocks give their first milk. It is the oldest continuously observed fact about her: whatever else changed, the first of February stayed hers.

lore.syncretism: Brigit's syncretic life runs in two directions. Across the water, her name is one with the goddess Brigantia of Roman Britain, honoured in inscriptions from the Wall country and portrayed on the Birrens relief with Minerva's globe and spear — the interpretatio romana pairing the exalted one with the Roman goddess of craft and war-wisdom; the tribal Brigantes and the Gaulish Brigindu carry the same name-element, and the old comparison with Sanskrit bṛhatī, 'the high, exalted one', shows how deep the root runs. Within Ireland, the identification is Christian: Brigit of Kildare, the sixth-century saint whose feast falls on Imbolc, whose church kept a perpetual fire, and whose wonder-tales in Cogitosus's Life echo the goddess's provinces. Whether saint succeeded goddess, goddess was Christianized into saint, or two figures fused in one name, the sources do not let us decide — and Mac Cana and Koch both counsel holding the question open. What is certain is the continuity of the name: the Exalted One never left Ireland's calendar.
lore.culturalLegacy: No Celtic deity has a longer unbroken afterlife. Imbolc is still celebrated as St Brigid's Day — Lá Fhéile Bríde — and since 2023 it has been a public holiday in the Republic of Ireland, the first named for a woman. Rushes are still woven into Brigid's crosses on the eve of the feast and hung above doors; hundreds of holy wells bear the saint's name, and the clootie and cure customs at them preserve the leech-sister's province in folk practice. Modern paganism and Celtic Reconstructionism restored the goddess explicitly, keeping Imbolc as the feast of the returning light and of the three crafts; poets, smiths, and healers alike claim her patronage. And the name itself — Brigid, Bridget, Bríd — never ceased to be given to Irish daughters, carrying the Proto-Celtic word for exaltation into every generation since the Iron Age.
lore.extendedMeditation: Brigit is the rare goddess whose three provinces are one act seen from three sides. The smith and the poet do the same thing: they take what is raw — ore, breath — and by heat and pressure give it a form that outlasts them. The healer does it too, coaxing the broken body back toward the shape it was made for. Cormac's three sisters are really a single lesson: that making is sacred wherever it happens, at the anvil, on the tongue, or at the sickbed. Her fire at Kildare, hedged and watched and never consumed, is the emblem of that lesson — a flame tended by nineteen keepers that still belongs, on the twentieth night, to the name itself. Craft, kept in common, does not go out.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Brigit — already plain ASCII in its modern scholarly spelling, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover (hence Tier 2 by the mechanical rule). The medieval manuscripts wrote the name in Insular script, the Irish hand of the Latin alphabet; in the older Ogham alphabet it would have been notched ᚁᚏᚔᚌᚔᚈ (B-R-I-G-I-T), a normalized reconstruction only — no Ogham stone records the theonym. Because the name is pure ASCII, its .com was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: brigid.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Brigit herself is unattested in pre-Christian Irish material: no Ogham stone, votive, or image names the goddess, and Ireland's Iron Age left no cult sites securely hers. Her name's material record lies across the water: Romano-British inscriptions honour Brigantia from the Wall country — most famously the relief from Birrens (Dumfriesshire), where the goddess stands with Minerva's globe, spear, and crown — and a Gaulish inscription from Volnay (Côte-d'Or) invokes Brigindu, the same name-element on the Continent. In Ireland the evidence is ecclesiastical and hydronymic: the monastic site of Kildare (Cill Dara, 'church of the oak'), with its round tower and its memory of the perpetual fire Giraldus describes, and the hundreds of holy wells dedicated to St Brigit, whose rag-trees and cure customs are the living deposit of the leech-sister's province.
